Project 1

Jason M. Klemm

2026-07-05

Task 1

To solve the overbooking problem first we need to define our parameters and create an objective function that can be used to find the optimal number of tickets to sell.

By definition we know that:

\(N\) = Maximum number of seats on the plane

\(n\) = Number of tickets sold

\(\gamma\) = The probability of overbooking the flight (i.e. the probability of more people showing up than seats on the plane when overbooked)

\(p\) = The probability that a ticket holder shows up for the flight

We know values for all parameters except \(n\), which is what we are after.

With this information we can also represent an individual ticket holder as the random variable \(Y\) that can take on the values of \(1\) for a show or \(0\) for a no-show to the flight. This then indicates a Bernoulli distribution, and if we let \(Y_i\) be the sum of all ticket holders represented as \(S\) then we have a Binomial distribution of \(n\) Bernoulli trials:

\[S = \sum_{i=1}^nY_i\]

In a discrete case our model can then be written as:

\[S\sim Bin(n,p)\]

However, there is also a way to solved this using a continuous model through the Normal Approximation to the Binomial. In this continuous case our model can be written as:

\[S\sim N(\mu,\sigma)\]

Where \(\mu = np\) and \(\sigma = \sqrt{(npq)}\), while also taking into careful consideration the continuity correction factor (\(+0.5\)) when calculating probabilities1.

With these both we can define some probabilities to help solve our problem with either case.

We know that the probability that \(S\), the number of ticket holders, is greater than \(N\), the number of seats on the plane, is \(\gamma\). So the probability we have is:

\[P(S>N)=\gamma\]

Through the complement probability we also know the probability of \(\gamma\) is equivalent to:

\[1 - P(S\le N) = \gamma\]

From here we just need to reason that in order to find the optimal amount of tickets to sell we need to minimize \(1 - P(S \le N)\) to where it is as close to \(\gamma\) as possible. This way we sell enough tickets to fill flight while also ensuring that we don’t observe too much overbooking.

To do this we rearrange and set the probability equation equal to \(0\):

\[1 - P(S\le N) - \gamma = 0\]

This then represents the Objective Function, and since we know all parameters except \(n\), we know that this is a function of \(n\), which we call \(f(n)\).

We can now begin to code this in R for each case, Discrete or Continuous, and solve the overbooking problem. It is also important to note that for each case we will need to find an integer value for number of tickets to sell since they cannot be sold in fractions.

Task 2

The discrete form of the objective function that can be used to solve this overbooking problem is:

\[1 - P(S\le N) - \gamma = 0 \space, \space \text{where} \space S\sim Bin(n,p)\]

This can be represented in R as 1 - pbinom(N, n, p) - gam. We use pbinom() because this is the R dpqr stem function that calculates the lower tail probability from a Binomial distribution by default.

Therefore in R we have:

\[f(n) = 1- \text{pbinom(N, n, p)} - \gamma = 0\]

where \(n\) is unknown and all other parameters are known.

Task 3

We can trial this discrete form of the objective function with the following parameters:

\(N = 200\)

\(p = 0.95\)

\(\gamma = 0.2\)

To get the optimal number tickets to sell I will make use of the which.min() function and get the index of the minimizing ticket number from a sequence of \(n\) values. The smallest number of tickets I would want to sell are the total number of seats on the plane \(N\), and the maximum I’ll set to \(N*1.10\), which means that we only to sell a maximum of \(10\%\) over the flight capacity which is reasonable. Furthermore to make use of the which.min() function I can find the absolute value of the resulting \(f(n)\) output first and then find where the function observes its smallest value. This value would then be where we see \(1 - P(S \le N)\) as close to \(\gamma\) as possible.

# Define function
obj_fun_discrete <- function(n, N, p, gam) {
  
 fnvals_discrete <- 1 - pbinom(N, n, p) - gam
 
 return(fnvals_discrete)
  
}

# Define known parameters
N <- 200
p <- 0.95
gam <- 0.2

# Define n range - floor to keep as integers
n_seq_discrete <- N:(floor(N*1.10))

# Calculate fnvals
fnvals_discrete <- obj_fun_discrete(n = n_seq_discrete, N = N, p = p, gam = gam)

# Get absolute values to assist in getting minimum value
abs_fnvals_discrete <- abs(fnvals_discrete)

# Get minimum index value of the absolute function
mins_discrete <- which.min(abs_fnvals_discrete)

# Get optimal ticket number
optimal_n_discrete <- n_seq_discrete[mins_discrete]

# Show result
print(optimal_n_discrete)
## [1] 208

Therefore we see that an optimal amount of tickets to sell is \(208\) for the given parameters. We can also visualize this process to help see how this process works and how we find the minimum value of \(f(n)\).

# Create the plot structure
plot(n_seq_discrete, fnvals_discrete, type = "n", 
     ylab = "Objective", xlab = "n",
     main = paste0("Objective Vs n to find optimal tickets sold\n(", optimal_n_discrete, ") gamma = ", gam, " N = ", N,  " discrete"))

# Add the dashed line connecting the raw function values
lines(n_seq_discrete, fnvals_discrete, lty = 2)

# Add the red points for the absolute value function
points(n_seq_discrete, abs_fnvals_discrete, pch = 21, bg = "red", col = "black")

# Add the blue points for the raw function
points(n_seq_discrete, fnvals_discrete, pch = 21, bg = "blue", col = "black")

# Add the horizontal zero line
abline(h = 0, col = "red")

# Add the vertical line at the optimal n
abline(v = optimal_n_discrete, col = "red")

In the plot you can see that the optimal ticket number is roughly where the objective function crosses the x-axis and where the absolute value of the objective function “bounces/skips/turns” off the x-axis and is minimized.

Task 4 and 5

The continuous form of the objective function that can be used to solve this overbooking problem is:

\[1 - P(S\le N) - \gamma = 0 \space, \space \text{where} \space S\sim N(\mu,\sigma)\]

This can be represented in R as 1 - pnorm(N, mu, sigma) - gam. We use pnorm() because this is the R dpqr stem function that calculates the lower tail probability from a Normal distribution by default.

Therefore in R we have:

\[f(n) = 1- \text{pnorm(N, mu, sigma)} - \gamma = 0\]

where \(n\) is unknown and all other parameters are known.

We can trial this continuous form of the objective function with the following parameters paying close attention to the fact that we need the continuity correction factor (\(+0.5\)) for \(N\):

\(N = 200\)

\(N_C = 200.5\)

\(p = 0.95\)

\(\gamma = 0.2\)

To get the optimal number tickets to sell for the continuous case I will first use a similar method as for the discrete case and then make use of the rootSolve::uniroot() function and get the roots of the function which will be the \(n\) values for which the function equals \(0\) (i.e. crosses the x-axis). Again, the smallest number of tickets I would want to sell are the total number of seats on the plane \(N\), and the maximum I’ll set to \(N*1.10\), which means that we only to sell a maximum of \(10\%\) over the flight capacity which is reasonable.

First using which.min() function to get the index of the minimizing ticket number from a sequence of \(n\) values.

# Define the continuous objective function
obj_fun_continuous <- function(n, N, p, gam) {
  Nc <- N + 0.5  # Continuity correction
  mus <- n * p # means
  sds <- sqrt(n * p * (1 - p)) # standard deviations
  
  fnvals_continuous <- 1 - pnorm(Nc, mus, sds) - gam
  
  return(fnvals_continuous)
}

# Define known parameters
N <- 200
p <- 0.95
gam <- 0.2

# Create a continuous sequence from n range
n_seq_continuous <- seq(N, floor(N*1.10), length.out = 10000)

# Calculate fnvals
fnvals_continuous <- obj_fun_continuous(n = n_seq_continuous, N = N, p = p, gam = gam)

# Get absolute values to assist in getting minimum value
abs_fnvals_continuous <- abs(fnvals_continuous)

# Get minimum index value of the absolute function
mins_continuous <- which.min(abs_fnvals_continuous)

# Get optimal ticket number
optimal_n_continuous <- n_seq_continuous[mins_continuous]

# Show result
print(optimal_n_continuous)
## [1] 208.2668

Therefore here we see that an optimal amount of tickets to sell is \(208.2668\) for the given parameters using the method we previously used for the discrete case. What we can gain from this is a value that will allow us to decide if we can do \(208\) or \(209\) depending on circumstances. Additionally we can again visualize this process to help see how this process works and how we find the minimum of \(f(n)\).

# Plot the curve
plot(n_seq_continuous, obj_fun_continuous(n_seq_continuous, N, p, gam), type = "l", 
     main = paste0("Objective Vs n to find optimal tickets sold\n(", round(optimal_n_continuous, 4), ") gamma = ", gam, " N = ", N,  " continuous"),
     xlab = "n", ylab = "Objective")

# Add the zero-line and the optimal n intersection
abline(h = 0, col = "blue")
abline(v = optimal_n_continuous, col = "blue")

Next using the rootSolve::uniroot() function:

# Find the root between set n range
root_n <- uniroot.all(obj_fun_continuous, interval = c(min(n_seq_continuous), max(n_seq_continuous)), N = N, p = p, gam = gam)

# Show result
print(root_n)
## [1] 208.2662

Therefore here we see that an optimal amount of tickets to sell is \(208.2662\) for the given parameters and that it is the only root and not an integer value. Again, what we can gain from this is a value that will allow us to decide if we can do \(208\) or \(209\) depending on circumstances (i.e. the returned root of the objective function can provide us with a value to base our final decision on). Additionally this is very close to the previous value we found of \(208.2668\) and we can again visualize this process to help see how this process works and how we find the root of \(f(n)\).

# Plot the curve
plot(n_seq_continuous, obj_fun_continuous(n_seq_continuous, N, p, gam), type = "l", 
     main = paste0("Objective Vs n to find optimal tickets sold\n(", round(root_n, 4), ") gamma = ", gam, " N = ", N,  " continuous"),
     xlab = "n", ylab = "Objective")

# Add the zero-line and the optimal n intersection
abline(h = 0, col = "blue")
abline(v = root_n, col = "blue")

In the plot you can see that the optimal ticket number is right where the objective function crosses the x-axis and is the root of the function (i.e. \(f(n)=0\))

Similar to how we solved the discrete case we can also use a different method that uses the absolute of the objective function here and its minimum using optimize(). This allows us to again find the minimum of the objective function where we see \(1 - P(S \le N)\) as close to \(\gamma\) as possible.

# Define the absolute value of the continuous case
abs_obj_fun_continuous <- function(n, N, p, gam) {
  abs(obj_fun_continuous(n, N, p, gam))
}

# Use optimise to find the minimum point
opt_result <- optimise(abs_obj_fun_continuous, interval = c(min(n_seq_continuous), max(n_seq_continuous)), N = N, p = p, gam = gam)

# optimise() returns a list; we want the 'minimum' value
print(opt_result$minimum)
## [1] 208.2662

As we can see we get the same exact result of \(208.2662\) as before. We can make the plot for this as well to visualize it.

# Plot the curve
plot(n_seq_continuous, abs_obj_fun_continuous(n_seq_continuous, N, p, gam), type = "l", 
     main = paste0("Abs Objective Vs n to find optimal tickets sold\n(", round(opt_result$minimum, 4), ") gamma = ", gam, " N = ", N,  " continuous"),
     xlab = "n", ylab = "Abs Objective")

# Add the zero-line and the optimal n intersection
abline(h = 0, col = "blue")
abline(v = opt_result$minimum, col = "blue")

Similar to the discrete case, you can see where the absolute value of the continuous objective function “bounces/skips/turns” off the x-axis and is minimized.

Task 6

Now that we have all of our solutions, equations and modeling complete it is wise to compile them all into one nice function with an informative output.

# Combine discrete and continuous functions - use nposs for clarity of what n should be
overbooking <- function(nposs, N, p, gam){
  
  ## Discrete case
  obj_fun_discrete <- function(n, N, p, gam) {
    
    fnvals_discrete <- 1 - pbinom(N, n, p) - gam
    
    return(fnvals_discrete)
    
  }
  
  # Calculate fnvals_discrete
  fnvals_discrete <- obj_fun_discrete(n = nposs, N = N, p = p, gam = gam)
  
  # Get absolute values to assist in getting minimum value
  abs_fnvals_discrete <- abs(fnvals_discrete)
  
  # Get minimum index value of the absolute function
  mins_discrete <- which.min(abs_fnvals_discrete)
  
  # Get optimal ticket number
  nd <- nposs[mins_discrete]
  
  # Create the plot for discrete
  plot(nposs, fnvals_discrete, type = "n", 
       ylab = "Objective", xlab = "n",
       main = paste0("Objective Vs n to find optimal tickets sold\n(", nd, ") gamma = ", gam, " N = ", N,  " discrete"))
  
  # Add the dashed line connecting the raw function values
  lines(nposs, fnvals_discrete, lty = 2)
  
  # Add the red points for the absolute value function
  points(nposs, abs_fnvals_discrete, pch = 21, bg = "red", col = "black")
  
  # Add the blue points for the raw function
  points(nposs, fnvals_discrete, pch = 21, bg = "blue", col = "black")
  
  # Add the horizontal zero line
  abline(h = 0, col = "red")
  
  # Add the vertical line at the optimal n
  abline(v = nd, col = "red")
  
  #############################################################
  
  ## Continuous case
  obj_fun_continuous <- function(n, N, p, gam) {
    Nc <- N + 0.5  # Continuity correction
    mus <- n * p # means
    sds <- sqrt(n * p * (1 - p)) # standard deviations
    
    fnvals_continuous <- 1 - pnorm(Nc, mus, sds) - gam
    
    return(fnvals_continuous)
  }
  
  nposs_continuous <- seq(min(nposs), max(nposs), length.out = 10000)
  
  # Calculate fnvals_discrete
  fnvals_continuous <- obj_fun_continuous(n = nposs_continuous, N = N, p = p, gam = gam)
  
  # Get absolute values to assist in getting minimum value
  abs_fnvals_continuous <- abs(fnvals_continuous)
  
  # Get minimum index value of the absolute function
  mins_continous <- which.min(abs_fnvals_continuous)
  
  # Get optimal ticket number
  nc <- nposs_continuous[mins_continous]
  
  # Find the root between set n range
  root <- uniroot.all(obj_fun_continuous, interval = c(min(nposs_continuous), max(nposs_continuous)), N = N, p = p, gam = gam)
  
  # Plot the curve for continuous
  plot(nposs_continuous, obj_fun_continuous(nposs_continuous, N, p, gam), type = "l", 
       main = paste0("Objective Vs n to find optimal tickets sold\n(", round(nc, 4), ") gamma = ", gam, " N = ", N,  " continuous"),
       xlab = "n", ylab = "Objective")
  
  # Add the zero-line and the optimal n intersection
  abline(h = 0, col = "blue")
  abline(v = nc, col = "blue")
  
  #############################################################
  
  ## Output
  
  out <- list(nd = nd, nc = nc, N = N, p = p, gamma = gam, root = root)
  
  return(out)
}

We can test the function to see if it works as intended:

# Test overbooking problem function
overbooking(nposs = 200:220, N = 200, p = 0.95, gam = 0.2)
